claim: Feeling of knowing after recall failure predicts later recognition above chance (Hart 1965) and carries real stored information; but Hart was read only via a secondary summary (Wikipedia).
agent_test: Ask agent for a pre-attempt feeling rating on questions, then compare to later correctness; AUROC vs a token-budget-matched baseline.

claim: Two-level monitoring/control framework (Nelson and Narens): monitor signals (ease-of-learning, JOL, FOK, confidence) feed control choices (allocate effort, stop search).
agent_test: Wire a pre-attempt difficulty signal to a budget decision; compare accuracy at equal tokens to fixed budget.

claim: Feelings of knowing can be driven by cue familiarity (question terms) rather than the stored answer; familiarity-based FOK is quick and fallible. Schwartz and Metcalfe (1992): priming cues raised FOK, a recall-boosting manipulation did not (4 experiments, abstract only).
agent_test: Build prompts with familiar terms but unanswerable content; check whether the pre-attempt gate overrates them.
audit_note: Schwartz & Metcalfe (1992) verified via Europe PMC abstract (four experiments; cue priming raised judgments, target generation did not; in Exp 3 target priming also raised them); Reder & Ritter (1992) confirmed to exist only through a citing record, abstract not read.

claim: Accessibility of partial information (right or wrong) also drives FOK; the interactive view says familiarity first, accessibility added when needed. LLM analogue: popularity predicts knowing.
agent_test: Compare a gate using only question text vs one allowed a short draft attempt; equal tokens.

claim: Judgments (confidence, FOK, JOL) reflect consistency among sampled cues; consensual answers get stronger judgments (FOK 91.2 vs 85.1, N=36; JOL 78.67 vs 62.99, N=24; children 73.22 vs 60.87, N=72). All from one author's group.
agent_test: Use agreement over k samples as confidence; compare to single verbalised confidence at equal tokens.

claim: Delayed JOLs (cue only, after a delay) predict recall far better than immediate JOLs for word pairs, mainly because delayed JOLs use a real retrieval attempt (gamma .72-.76 vs .36). Dunlosky and Nelson (1992): robust when the cue is the stimulus alone (45 of 45 subjects), small or absent with the full pair as cue.
agent_test: Judge difficulty after a short unaided attempt rather than from the prompt alone; compare AUROC.
audit_note: Minor slip: Kimball & Metcalfe's delayed cue-only .72 (Exp 2) is compared with delayed cue-target .43, not immediate .36 (that comparison is Exp 3, .76 vs .36); Rhodes & Tauber's cue-only g=0.03 and Dunlosky & Nelson '45 of 45 subjects' verified. Kimball & Metcalfe attribute the retrieval-attempt advantage to a memory boost rather than better monitoring.

claim: The delayed-JOL advantage depends on the retrieval attempt: it vanishes if targets are re-shown (.53 vs .43 n.s.), and part of it is selection of recall outcomes.
agent_test: Ablate: give the answer along with the question when rating; check the gate loses accuracy.
audit_note: Kimball & Metcalfe verified (reexposure erased the effect: Exp 3 delayed .53 vs immediate .43 n.s.; Exp 2 .39 vs .46); 'selection of recall outcomes' is their memory hypothesis (retrieved items get a spaced-study boost).

claim: The delayed-JOL advantage does not carry to text passages (immediate prediction with immediate test was best; N=96).
agent_test: Test the gate on long multi-step tasks vs short facts; check where it fails.

claim: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) meta-analysis: delayed JOLs raise relative accuracy a lot (g = 0.93, 4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes) but raise memory itself only a little (g = 0.08, 3,807 participants, 98 effect sizes). The g = .70 and .03 values quoted in Tekin and Roediger are not in the abstract and stay unverified.
agent_test: Open the original before using any number.
audit_note: Rhodes & Tauber abstract numbers verified; the 0.70 and 0.03 values are in Tekin & Roediger's introduction (not the R&T abstract), as the claim says.

claim: Making JOLs changes later memory (reactivity): small, unstable, and depends on item type (related pairs up d=0.38-0.43; unrelated pairs down d=0.41-0.80; a direct online replication with N=41 differs from the within-subject result).
agent_test: Run the agent with and without an extra self-rating step at equal tokens; measure accuracy change.

claim: Judgments of learning are influenced by superficial cues that need not help memory: type size raises predicted but not actual memory (Kornell et al. 2011), and the role of metamemory beliefs in the font-size effect depends on word frequency (beliefs mediate it for low-frequency words, not high-frequency ones; Fan et al. 2021). For naturalistic scene pictures, JOLs use several intrinsic and extrinsic cues, most of which also predict recognition (Undorf & Broder 2021).
agent_test: Vary surface features (length, formatting, jargon) with difficulty fixed; check gate sensitivity.
audit_note: Undorf & Broder report that scene JOLs rest on cues most of which also predicted actual recognition (not cues that fail to help memory); in the font-size study (first author Fan, not Tian) word frequency moderates the contribution of beliefs, not the font-size effect itself; only Kornell et al. show a cue (type size) that moves predicted but not actual memory.
claim_before_audit: Judgments are driven by superficial cues that do not help memory (font size raises JOLs, moderated by word frequency; scene pictures use intrinsic and extrinsic cues).

claim: Large LMs are well calibrated on lettered multiple choice and true/false, improving with size and few-shot prompts (Kadavath, up to 52B).
agent_test: Reproduce P(True) on our model at equal tokens.

claim: A value head trained on bare questions (P(IK)) predicts correctness before answering; AUROC rises with size and transfers partly out of distribution (TriviaQA-only: LAMBADA .864, Python .928; all-task: .987/.853) but is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Training on all tasks lifts AUROC to .75-.99; TriviaQA-only gives .61-.93 (column labels uncertain).
agent_test: Train a small probe on our agent's easy/hard labels from past runs; evaluate on held-out task classes.

claim: P(IK) moves in the right direction with relevant context and hints, as accessibility accounts predict; models predict their own P(IK) slightly better than another model does.
agent_test: Add retrieved context and watch the gate shift.

claim: Showing many own samples improves self-evaluation (consistency cue); 5-sample consistency raises GSM8K failure-prediction AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7% (checked in the paper table).
agent_test: Compare single verbalised confidence vs 5-sample agreement at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Xiong et al. Table 3 verified (GPT-3.5 only: CoT top-K M=1 54.8 to 5-sample consistency 92.7 AUROC on GSM8K); Kadavath et al. section 4.2 confirms showing many own samples improves self-evaluation.

claim: Verbalised confidence from black-box LLMs is overconfident and a weak failure predictor: GPT-3/3.5/Vicuna mean ECE above 0.377; GPT-4 mean AUROC 62.7% (near chance). Checked in paper.
agent_test: Check our agent's verbalised confidence AUROC on own tasks.
audit_note: ECE above 0.377 (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna) and GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% verified in Xiong et al. text; Yona et al. abstract-level only (one lab's paper counted once for the numbers).

claim: For RLHF models, asked-for verbal probabilities beat token probabilities (gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE .140 to .050, AUC .869 to .894; GPT-4 ECE .078 to .024), but on adversarial TruthfulQA AUC stays weak (.485-.622). Checked in paper table. Note: this conflicts in tone with Xiong (verbal AUROC near chance): ECE improves, discrimination does not.
agent_test: Elicit top-k guesses plus probabilities; compare ECE and AUROC at equal tokens.

claim: Finetuning on about 1,000 graded examples gives better uncertainty than prompting; prompted ECE does not improve as base models improve; a model can estimate other models' uncertainty. Shift test: LoRA+Prompt AUROC 80.0 / 85.1 / 70.2 vs zero-shot 56.9 / 66.2 / 47.1 (LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, coding); ECE worsened for two of the three.
agent_test: Fit a small calibration layer on our agent's own history (about 1,000 labelled runs).
audit_note: Kapoor et al. Table 3 verified (AUROC 80.0/85.1/70.2 vs 56.9/66.2/47.1; ECE worse for LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct); all specifics come from one paper, with Lin et al. (2022) supporting finetuned verbalized uncertainty only generally.

claim: Models can recognise unanswerable questions but below humans (GPT-4 F1 75.47 vs human 84.93; 1,032 unanswerable, 2,337 answerable). Checked in paper.
agent_test: Include unanswerable items; check that the gate says refuse/defer.

claim: Aligning to a model-specific known/unknown set (Idk) or refusal data makes the model refuse unknowns, with an alignment tax (Idk-SFT truthful 74.75% vs prompting 66.93%).
agent_test: Use own known/unknown history to train the abstain decision.

claim: Semantic entropy over sampled answers predicts correctness better than sequence likelihood (AUROC about .78 TriviaQA, read from text; figure not checked).
agent_test: Cluster samples by meaning for the vote; compare to string match.

claim: Internal states carry knowledge-state signals: entity-recognition latents in SAEs (causal steering to refuse), error probes concentrate at exact-answer tokens but do not transfer across datasets, SAPLMA 71-83%.
agent_test: Not testable on an API-only agent; note for model choice.
audit_note: Orgad abstract confirms concentration in specific tokens and failure to generalize across datasets (exact-answer-token detail is from the paper body, not the abstract); Azaria 71-83% and Ferrando refusal steering verified.

claim: Popularity of the subject predicts whether a model knows a fact; scaling does not help the long tail; adaptive retrieval below a popularity threshold helps. Fine-tuning on unknown facts is learned slower and raises hallucination.
agent_test: Use entity rarity as a gate feature.

claim: A trained complexity router (Adaptive-RAG) is a machine ease-of-learning gate; routing errors cost accuracy (oracle router 45.00 vs learned 37.17 F1 in one column).
agent_test: Build router, measure vs always-deep at equal tokens.

claim: Naming the skill or problem type before solving helps (11.6% over CoT on MATH; the comparison baselines for the 3.5% figure are stated inconsistently in the paper).
agent_test: Compare typed-prompt retrieval vs plain CoT at equal tokens.

claim: Hedging wording does not track knowledge: epistemic markers shift accuracy (more than 80% variation, high-certainty markers lower accuracy by 7%); models do not faithfully express uncertainty.
schema_part: G (do not prompt with certainty words)
agent_test: Remove certainty words from scaffold prompts; measure accuracy.
audit_note: Abstract-level verification only; the 'does not track knowledge' framing is the authors' hypothesis that models mimic observed language use.

claim: People over-trust default LLM answers: human AUC .589/.602/.592 vs model confidence AUC .751/.746/.781 (checked); matching explanation tone to model confidence narrows both gaps.
agent_test: Show calibrated hedges to raters; measure discrimination.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLM judgments of learning did not predict human recognition for garden-path sentences (all LLM slope CIs include zero; humans B=.167 [.018,.316], N=78; checked).
agent_test: Do not assume human-like item difficulty ratings from the model.

claim: Models predict their own behaviour better than another model can (self 48.5-49.6% vs cross 35.2-36.2% plateau, checked), suggesting privileged self-access. Paper text also gives 31.8% for GPT-4o on Llama; the +17% headline compares a specific pair. New: Kapoor found Mistral-7B features predicted LLaMA-2 7B better than LLaMA-2 itself, and Kadavath found no self-advantage on model A's data (AUROC .8633 vs .8631). Privileged access is weak and task dependent.
agent_test: Train a self-predictor; compare to a second model at equal tokens.

claim: Human ease-of-learning judgments (made before study) are the weakest of the standard metamemory judgments at predicting later memory and correlate only weakly with judgments of knowing (Leonesio and Nelson 1990, abstract only). Underwood (1966) was not found.
agent_test: Compare the prompt-only ease rating with a past pass rate per task class and with a short draft, on the same tasks.

claim: Base-rate item difficulty (how often others got the item right) predicted memory better than a person's own feeling of knowing, which beat normative FOK ratings (Nelson et al. 1986, abstract only, no numbers). Past pass rate per task class is therefore a strong gate candidate.
agent_test: Keep a table of pass rates by task class; test it against the model's own ease rating.

claim: Ease and FOK judgments steer study time to harder items, but extra time can give little or no recall gain (labor in vain, Nelson and Leonesio 1988, abstract only).
agent_test: Cap extra compute on items flagged hard; measure gain per token.

claim: Fluent surface features inflate human predictions without helping memory: type size changed JOLs but not recall; study repetitions changed recall but barely changed JOLs (Kornell et al. 2011); strong pair association seen at study inflates JOLs against a weak cue-alone link (Koriat and Bjork 2005). Effect sizes not obtained. Whether fluency inflates LLM self-ratings was not found.
agent_test: Rate the same problems with and without a visible worked solution or a polished rewrite; compare self-rating and accuracy.

claim: Pooled absolute FOK accuracy in young adults was not found. A 2023 meta-analysis (20 studies) gives only age differences: episodic FOK g = 0.53 (older worse), semantic FOK g = -0.10 (no difference), with publication bias for episodic FOK.
agent_test: Do not quote a human FOK accuracy figure. Measure the agent's own.

claim: Reasoning models verbalise confidence better than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings (six open 32B-class models), because of slow-thinking behaviour; calibration improves as the chain of thought unfolds.
schema_part: S0 gate placement (read confidence after thinking)
agent_test: Compare confidence read before vs after the draft on our runs.

claim: Evidence on whether thinking longer helps calibration is split: Yoon et al. find better calibration along the chain; Mei et al. find reasoning models often above 85% confidence on wrong answers and more overconfident with deeper reasoning. No 2025-2026 frontier AUROC above GPT-4's 62.7% was confirmed here.
agent_test: Measure verbalised-confidence AUROC at several reasoning budgets on our own tasks.

claim: Hidden-state probes trained on at most 1,000 examples predict correctness well in-distribution (AUC above .7; above .9 for one model on AIME) and give 24% token savings in early exit at 88.2% vs 88.6% accuracy, but transfer across task classes is partial: math to math AUC .69-.83, math to logic .56-.63, logic to math .74-.77 but with ECE .17-.19, and ECE degrades on AIME (.25-.31).
agent_test: Train a gate on ~1,000 graded runs; test on a held-out task class; reset the threshold when the class changes.
audit_note: In Zhang et al. Table 2 (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) math-to-math transfer AUC runs 0.69-0.83 (GSM8K to AIME is 0.69), not .76-.83; the other figures (math to logic .56-.63, logic to math .74-.77 with ECE .17-.19, AIME ECE .25-.31, early exit 88.2% vs 88.6% at 24% savings) check out.
claim_before_audit: Hidden-state probes trained on at most 1,000 examples predict correctness well in-distribution (AUC above .7; above .9 for one model on AIME) and give 24% token savings in early exit at 88.2% vs 88.6% accuracy, but transfer across task classes is partial: math to math AUC .76-.83, math to logic .56-.63, logic to math .74-.77 but with ECE .17-.19, and ECE degrades on AIME (.25-.31).

claim: Probes read at the end of the question (before the answer) are weaker than probes read at the exact answer token (AUC .72-.80 vs .83-.95), which supports a short draft before the judgment over a pure pre-attempt gate. A head-to-head at equal tokens for frontier models was NOT found.
agent_test: Run the pre-attempt gate and a 200-token draft judge on the same tasks at equal tokens.

claim: Self-knowledge fails on long outputs and complex tasks in LLMs (Binder: models failed to beat baselines when the response was long), an indirect analogue of Maki's (1998) text failure. Not tested directly for metamemory-style gates.
agent_test: Check gate accuracy separately by output length bucket.

claim: Human-labelled difficulty is linearly decodable from LLM hidden states (AMC rho about .88, 60 models); difficulty derived from the model's own failures is weaker and degrades under RL. Surface-cue control (length) was not confirmed.
agent_test: Probe for human-difficulty vs failure-based difficulty; control for prompt length.

claim: Pairwise relative confidence (which of two questions will I get right) beat absolute verbalised confidence by 3.5% AUC on average and self-consistency by 1.7% across five frontier models and 14 tasks, at a higher call cost.
agent_test: Rank candidate tasks against a bank of past outcomes by pairwise comparison.

claim: A trained pre-answer difficulty policy can save compute: AdaptThink cut response length 53% and raised accuracy 2.4% for a 1.5B model on math.
agent_test: Train or prompt a think/no-think choice; compare tokens and accuracy with always-think.
